quote: Lives saved don’t diminish in marginal utility, so this is an appropriate calculation.
content: This parenthesis is the entire disputed premise, asserted in passing as though it were a housekeeping note. Linearity in lives is what makes 450 expected lives beat 400 certain ones; someone with a concave utility over lives saved — which is what risk aversion about a rescue operation amounts to — prefers option 1 without any incoherence, and nothing in decision theory forbids that shape. Note also that the original experiment this is adapted from, Tversky and Kahneman's Asian disease problem (1981), used options with identical expected values, precisely so that the demonstration would not depend on any assumption about the utility of lives. Rewriting it so that one option dominates in expectation makes the choice look foolish only to a reader who has already granted the premise the essay is arguing for.

quote: Then a majority choose option 2. Even though it’s the same gamble.
content: This part is solid, and it is the strongest thing in the essay. The reflection of preference between gain-framed and loss-framed descriptions of the same distribution is one of the findings that survived the replication crisis intact: the Asian disease problem was replicated with a large effect size across dozens of samples in the Many Labs project (Klein et al. 2014), unlike much of the social-psychological literature of the same vintage. The inconsistency across frames is a genuine defect and cannot be defended as a preference, since no preference over outcomes can depend on which of two logically equivalent sentences the experimenter uttered. What the framing result does not establish is which of the two frames gives the right answer — only that at most one of them can.

quote: If you assign any negative value to hiccups, then, on pain of decision-theoretic incoherence, there must be some number of hiccups that would add up to rival the negative value of a shark attack.
content: "On pain of decision-theoretic incoherence" is too strong: what the argument actually requires is the Archimedean or continuity axiom, and denying continuity costs you a real-valued utility representation, not coherence. Lexicographic preferences are complete and transitive, admit no cycles, and cannot be money-pumped; they simply cannot be written as a single real number, which is a limitation of the notation rather than a demonstrated defect in the agent. The philosophical literature on incommensurability and parity (Chang's Incommensurability, Incomparability, and Practical Reason, 1997 — a book, no DOI) exists precisely because this move is contested. There is a serious case for aggregating small harms, and this sentence isn't it: it declares the opponent incoherent by naming an axiom they reject.

quote: Research shows that people distinguish “sacred values,” like human lives, from “unsacred values,” like money.
content: The research is Tetlock's taboo-tradeoff work (Tetlock et al. 2000) and Baron and Spranca on protected values, and neither concludes what the essay wants. Tetlock's account is that the outrage is functional: refusing to price a sacred value is how people signal that a relationship is not a market, and the moral-outrage-plus-cleansing response is a relational commitment display, not an arithmetic failure. The same literature also found that so-called protected values are routinely traded off once the choice is framed as a tragic tradeoff between two sacred values rather than as a taboo one, and that people abandon them under mild probing. The finding is that people manage sacred values contextually — which is a poorer fit for "the brain cannot multiply" than for "the brain is doing something else here."

quote: My favorite anecdote along these lines comes from a team of researchers who evaluated the effectiveness of a certain project
content: No researchers, agency, country, or date are named, and the story is doing evidential work: it is the essay's only instance of sacred-value thinking causing real deaths. The generalization it supports is also false about actual governments. Every economically significant US regulation since the early 1980s has been evaluated with an explicit value of a statistical life — currently around $11 million in Department of Transportation guidance and in the same range at the EPA — and the UK's NICE has published an explicit cost-per-QALY threshold for two decades. Bureaucracies put dollar figures on lives constantly and in public; what they decline to do is say so in press releases, which is a fact about rhetoric, and the essay has already explained why rhetoric works that way.

quote: Should I organize a $700,000 fundraiser to pay for a single bone marrow transplant, or should I use that same money on mosquito nets and prevent the malaria deaths of some 200 children?
content: The implied figure of $3,500 per death averted is in the range GiveWell has published for bed nets, so the arithmetic is not invented — but the estimate carries an uncertainty the sentence hides. GiveWell's own cost-per-life-saved figures for the Against Malaria Foundation have moved by more than a factor of two across revisions as insecticide resistance, net durability, baseline mortality, and the counterfactual funding picture were re-estimated, and GiveWell explicitly cautions against treating the number as a purchase price. The comparison is also not between a transplant and nets in general but between one identified patient and a statistical projection over a distribution of futures. That asymmetry in evidential quality is exactly what the essay's opponents point at, and it deserves an answer rather than a round number.

quote: But altruism isn’t the warm fuzzy feeling you get from being altruistic. If you’re doing it for the spiritual benefit, that is nothing but selfishness.
content: On the essay's own consequentialist terms this is a risky prescription rather than an obvious one. The economics of giving has modelled donors as impurely altruistic since Andreoni's warm-glow papers (Economic Journal 100, 1990), and the empirical result is that the warm glow is what most giving runs on: fundraising that removes the personal, emotional, identified-victim element reliably raises less money, and Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic found that simply teaching donors about scope insensitivity reduced giving to the identified victim without raising giving to statistics. A movement that shames the motive it depends on may end up moving less money, which is a consequence the essay's own framework has to count. "The primary thing is to help others, whatever the means" and "do not enjoy it" are in tension when enjoyment is one of the means.
